Chapter 4: Why Good Intentions Can Lead to Tyranny
Let’s take a closer look at something that might surprise you—the paradox of good intentions.
Now, a lot of folks who believe in central planning really do want to make life better. They dream of ending poverty, shrinking the gap between rich and poor, and building a more just world. And honestly, those are goals we can all admire—they speak to some of our deepest values.
But here’s the twist: when you try to achieve these goals by handing the state unlimited power, things often take a turn for the worse.
Why is that? Well, it starts with how planning works. To make their vision a reality, planners have to make choices for everyone. They decide what’s best—even when people have other ideas. It’s not just about being smart or having the right data. It’s about having the authority to make folks go along, whether they want to or not.
And the bigger the goal, the tighter the grip has to be.
Think of it like this: imagine a gardener standing in a wild, beautiful meadow. At first, they just pull a few weeds and trim some bushes—nothing major. The meadow still thrives. But as the gardener’s ambitions grow, they start rearranging everything to fit their own perfect plan. Soon, that wild diversity fades away. Instead of a lively meadow, you get a garden that reflects only the gardener’s taste—not the magic of nature itself.
Central planning works much the same way. It replaces the spontaneous order of society—the way people naturally organize and pursue their own goals—with a single, top-down vision. Suddenly, the diversity of ideas and values gets brushed aside for the sake of uniformity. And anyone who pushes back? They’re seen as getting in the way.
That’s where things get dangerous. At first, disagreement might be met with friendly persuasion or education. But if people don’t fall in line, those in charge may turn to stricter measures—coercion, even punishment. The planners, convinced they’re doing the right thing, start to believe that any means are justified by their noble ends. And just like that, the line between helping and harming gets blurry.
History has plenty of examples. In some places, efforts to create equality led to targeting people seen as privileged—or just stubborn. Elsewhere, the drive for order and efficiency meant shutting down independent groups, silencing critics, or even jailing dissenters. The common thread? The belief that the state always knows best, and that individual rights can be set aside for the so-called greater good.
Of course, this doesn’t mean every kind of collective action is risky. Societies need rules, institutions, and shared values to work together. The real trouble starts when the state claims the right to control every part of life, treating every disagreement as a threat instead of a chance to improve.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Good intentions just aren’t enough. How we pursue justice and equality matters just as much as the goals themselves. If we let the state go unchecked, even the best plans can slide into oppression. The challenge is finding ways to build a fairer world—without giving up the freedom that makes justice and equality possible in the first place.
